intro:
The exercises in this chapter are about decisions you make before any business logic exists: where to draw crate boundaries, how wide to open a module's visibility, when a Cargo feature is the right tool versus when it is a trap, and which dependencies a core crate is allowed to know about. None of these are aesthetic choices. Each one fixes the direction of your dependency graph, the size of your stable API surface, and the reproducibility of your builds for as long as the repository lives.

The through-line is restraint. Start with fewer crates than your C++/C#/Go instincts suggest, keep visibility as narrow as a real caller forces it to be, prefer additive features to mode matrices, and keep the domain crate ignorant of HTTP and SQL. The lab and the feature-matrix exercise both push the same point: a compile-time switch that has to be evaluated once for the whole build graph is the wrong place to encode a per-request or per-environment mode. Get those boundaries right and the rest of the book has somewhere clean to live.

exerciseSolutions.title: Name the unit before you design it
exerciseSolutions.solution:
First fix the four words so they stop being synonyms. A package is what Cargo manages from one Cargo.toml; it is the unit of versioning and publishing. A crate is what the compiler builds in one pass; it is the unit of compilation and the unit of the visibility system (pub means visible outside this crate). A module is a tree of names inside a single crate; it is purely an organizational and visibility device with no separate build or dependency story. A workspace groups packages so they share one Cargo.lock, one target directory, and one top-level command. The nesting is strict: a workspace contains packages, each package produces one or more crates, and each crate contains a module tree.

For the inherited repository, classify by asking what actually needs isolation. The API service, the worker, and the CLI are three binaries with genuinely different dependency sets and different release cadences, so each justifies its own crate (and, in a workspace, its own package). The shared domain models are reused by all three and benefit from a stable, infrastructure-free public surface, so they belong in their own library crate that everyone depends on. That is the boundary justified by dependency and API isolation, not by folder preference: the domain crate must not pull in the API's HTTP stack or the worker's queue client.

Which boundaries are only organizational and should stay modules? Anything inside one of those crates. The API's routing, request validation, and serialization layers are modules within the api crate, not separate crates, because splitting them buys no dependency isolation and only adds Cargo.toml files, version bumps, and slower incremental builds. The CLI's argument parsing and its command handlers are modules within the cli crate for the same reason. A directory boundary is not automatically a crate boundary; reach for a new crate only when it gives you a real seam (dependency isolation, compile-time separation, a stable reusable surface, or a clean public/private split), and reach for a module when the only thing you want is tidier names.

Which boundary belongs at workspace scope rather than crate scope? The shared policy across all of these: the single lockfile that pins one resolved dependency graph for the whole product, the shared target directory, the workspace-level dependency declarations that let every member agree on one version of serde or tokio, and the top-level cargo check --workspace that builds everything at once. Those concerns are about the product as a whole, not about any single crate, so they live in the workspace root Cargo.toml.
criteria: Package (one Cargo.toml, versioned), crate (one compilation unit and the visibility boundary), module (names inside a crate), and workspace (shared lock/target/commands) are each given distinct definitions.
The domain crate is split out specifically to isolate it from the API's and worker's dependencies, an argument from dependency isolation rather than folder layout.
Routing, validation, and CLI command handlers are explicitly kept as modules inside their crates because a separate crate would add cost without buying isolation.

exerciseSolutions.title: Read the public surface from a module tree
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Start from what a downstream crate can actually see. The only thing that crosses the crate boundary is what is reachable through a pub path from the crate root. Here the root re-exports two names, so a downstream caller imports exactly `use your_crate::OrderId;` and `use your_crate::OrderService;`. They do not import `your_crate::domain::OrderId` or `your_crate::service::OrderService`, and they cannot reach anything under the internal adapter modules at all, because those modules are not pub from the root. The flat, root-level path is the stable promise; the deep internal path is an implementation detail they never name.

That distinction is exactly what gives you refactoring room. Because callers depend on the re-exported names and not on the internal layout, the module names domain and service may be renamed, merged, or reorganized freely as long as the crate root keeps re-exporting OrderId and OrderService from wherever they now live. You could move OrderId into a types module, split service into two modules, or restructure the adapters entirely, and no downstream code breaks, because none of those internal names were ever part of the public surface. The pub use at the root is the seam: internal modules stay deep and specific while the public API stays small and calm.

This is why pub(crate) is usually the better first choice than pub. A public path is an API promise even when it felt temporary the day you wrote it; once another crate imports it, widening was easy and narrowing is a breaking change. pub(crate) lets an item be used freely throughout your own crate while keeping it invisible across the crate boundary, so you keep full freedom to change it. The maintenance cost of reaching for full pub too early is that you convert an internal helper into a contract you must support, version, and reason about on every future change; you pay that cost forever, often for a type you only needed two modules over. Climb the visibility ladder one rung at a time, and shape the external surface deliberately with pub use rather than by leaving everything pub by default.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Root re-exports define the public path; mod adapters stays internal and free to change.
criteria: The stable import paths are identified as your_crate::OrderId and your_crate::OrderService at the crate root, not the deep module paths.
Re-exporting is shown to hide the domain/service/adapters layout so those internal modules can be renamed or reorganized without breaking callers.
Widening to pub too early is described as turning an internal helper into a permanent contract, making pub(crate) the safer default.

exerciseSolutions.title: Create a workspace layout for a multi-crate product
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Use one workspace root whose only job is to list members, pin one Cargo.lock, and centralize shared dependency versions. Underneath it, give each component its own package. The shared business types go in a domain library crate. Infrastructure code goes in an adapters library crate that implements traits the domain defines (a database repository, an HTTP or message-queue client). The two long-running processes, api and worker, are binary crates, and there is a small cli binary for support tasks. The dependency direction is the whole point: api, worker, and cli depend on adapters and domain; adapters depends on domain; domain depends on nothing in the workspace and on no infrastructure crate at all.

Concretely, domain owns the order, account, and policy types plus the trait definitions like OrderRepository, and its Cargo.toml contains only lightweight, semantically neutral dependencies (something like serde for shape, perhaps thiserror for its own error type). It must not list reqwest, sqlx, axum, or a tracing subscriber. The adapters crate is where sqlx, an HTTP client, and the concrete tracing wiring live, because that is the crate allowed to know about wire formats and storage. The api binary depends on axum and on domain and adapters, wires a concrete repository into the domain's services, and serves requests; the worker binary depends on its queue client plus domain and adapters; the cli depends on clap plus domain and adapters. The arrows all point inward toward domain, never outward from it.

Centralize shared versions with [workspace.dependencies] in the root Cargo.toml so every member agrees on one serde and one tokio, and have each crate opt in with serde = { workspace = true }. Commit Cargo.lock at the root so production resolves the exact same graph every build.

The tradeoff to state plainly: splitting into four-plus crates costs you more Cargo.toml ceremony and makes a cross-cutting change touch several crates at once, but it buys two things that matter for a product. First, dependency hygiene: the domain crate physically cannot accumulate infrastructure dependencies, because they are not in its manifest, so the temptation that ruins prototypes is removed by construction. Second, build and API benefits: changing an adapter does not force a recompile of the domain's public types, and the domain's surface stays small and stable enough to reuse. If the product were small, fewer crates with the same internal module boundaries would be cheaper; the multi-crate layout earns its keep precisely when independent dependency sets and release policy diverge.
exerciseSolutions.code:
# Cargo.toml (workspace root)
[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = ["domain", "adapters", "api", "worker", "cli"]

[workspace.dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros"] }
thiserror = "1"

# domain/Cargo.toml  -> library, no infrastructure deps
[package]
name = "domain"
[dependencies]
serde = { workspace = true }
thiserror = { workspace = true }
# NOTE: no sqlx, no reqwest, no axum here. That isolation is the design.

# adapters/Cargo.toml -> implements domain traits over real infra
[package]
name = "adapters"
[dependencies]
domain = { path = "../domain" }
sqlx = "0.7"
# reqwest 0.12 needs explicit features and a tokio runtime in a real build,
# e.g. reqwest = { version = "0.12", features = ["json"] }; features omitted here for brevity.
reqwest = "0.12"

# api/Cargo.toml -> binary depends inward
[package]
name = "api"
[dependencies]
domain = { path = "../domain" }
adapters = { path = "../adapters" }
axum = "0.7"
tokio = { workspace = true }
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Workspace manifests showing the inward dependency direction; domain lists no infrastructure crates.
criteria: The layout has a workspace root plus separate domain, adapters, api, worker, and cli packages.
The domain crate's manifest lists only neutral dependencies and explicitly excludes sqlx/reqwest/axum, keeping it infrastructure-free.
api, worker, and cli depend on adapters and domain while domain depends on nothing in the workspace, so dependencies point inward.
The stated tradeoff weighs extra manifest ceremony and cross-crate changes against guaranteed dependency hygiene and smaller recompiles plus a stable domain surface.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair a feature flag matrix without turning Cargo into a mode engine
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Name the defect precisely. The crate encodes three mutually exclusive operational modes (sqlite, postgres, memory) as Cargo features and assumes exactly one is enabled. This fights the resolver on two fronts. First, Cargo features are additive by design: anything in the dependency graph can turn a feature on, and the resolver unions all requests, so you cannot rely on exactly one being active. If two consumers each enable a different backend, you get both, and your one-of-three assumption silently breaks. Second, a feature is resolved once for the entire build graph before the compiler runs, so it can only answer compile-time questions. The backend a service should use is a deployment question that can differ per environment and even per run, which a single compile-time choice cannot represent.

The fix is to move the mode out of features and into runtime configuration, while keeping compile-time options only for what genuinely affects which code is built. Decide which backends are even compiled into this binary, and then choose among the compiled ones at startup from config. A clean shape is a runtime Backend enum chosen from an environment variable or config file, constructed once and passed inward. Optional dependencies still belong in features: if a deployment never needs Postgres, keep a postgres feature that gates the sqlx Postgres driver so it is not compiled or shipped. That preserves additive capability (turning postgres on adds a capability, it never removes sqlite), which is exactly how features are supposed to compose.

Reject impossible combinations early and explicitly rather than letting them reach a query. Parse the configured backend into the enum at startup; an unknown value, or a backend that was not compiled into this build, is a hard configuration error reported before the service accepts traffic. That is the runtime analogue of the lab: validate the selection up front and return a clear error for anything that is not exactly one valid choice, instead of assuming the environment is well-formed. So: which parts stay compile-time? Only whether a given backend driver is built in at all, expressed as an additive optional dependency. Which parts move to runtime? The actual backend selection, because it varies per environment and the feature resolver cannot express per-deployment choice.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Backend choice moves to a validated runtime enum; only the optional driver stays a Cargo feature.
criteria: The answer explains that features are additive and resolved once per build graph, so mutually exclusive modes cannot be guaranteed and cannot vary per environment.
Additive capability is preserved by keeping the Postgres driver behind an optional feature that adds, never removes, a backend.
Impossible or unbuilt selections are validated at startup via Backend::from_config, which returns an explicit error before the service runs.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose a dependency policy for shared crates
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The policy in one sentence: the core domain crate knows business concepts first and infrastructure concepts last, so protocol and storage dependencies move outward into adapter crates and only business-meaningful types live inward. The three prototype shortcuts each violate this and each has a specific home. The HTTP status type is a transport detail; it moves out to the API adapter crate, where the HTTP layer already lives. The database error type is a storage detail; it moves out to the persistence adapter crate. The tracing crate dependency, if it brought a subscriber or transport, moves out too; if the domain wants to emit events it can depend on a thin facade rather than a concrete tracing backend, and the wiring to an actual collector lives in an adapter or the binary. The result is that the domain crate's Cargo.toml stops listing reqwest/axum, the database driver, and the tracing subscriber.

Moving the dependencies out is only half the job; you also need translation boundaries so the infrastructure types do not leak inward through return types. The clearest one is errors. The persistence adapter implements a domain-defined trait such as OrderRepository, catches the database error type internally, and converts it into a domain error like RepositoryError::NotFound or RepositoryError::Conflict before returning. The domain never sees the storage error; it sees a business-meaningful failure it can actually reason about. The same translation happens at the API edge: the adapter maps a domain error to an HTTP status, so the status type lives where HTTP lives and never travels inward. These conversions are the seams that let you swap Postgres for something else, or HTTP for a queue, without touching the domain.

On the shared utility crate: allow one only when it removes real duplication behind a stable, narrow surface, and refuse to let it become a junk drawer. A shared crate of genuinely cross-cutting value types (a validated identifier newtype, a money type, a time helper used identically by several crates) is justified because the alternative is copy-paste that drifts. What is not justified is a util crate that accumulates whatever was convenient, because then every member crate depends on everything and you have recreated the coupling you split crates to avoid. The test is concrete: if you cannot describe the shared crate's purpose in one sentence without the word miscellaneous, it should not exist yet. Keep the domain dependency-light, translate infrastructure types at the boundary, and gate shared crates on real, named duplication.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The domain exposes a business error; adapters translate storage and HTTP types at the boundary.
criteria: The HTTP status type and database error type are moved out of the domain crate into the API and persistence adapter crates respectively.
A concrete translation boundary is given: the persistence adapter converts the database error into a domain RepositoryError so storage types never travel inward.
A shared utility crate is permitted only for named, real duplication behind a narrow surface and explicitly rejected as a default catch-all bucket.

exerciseSolutions.title: Write the CI command pack for the chapter examples
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Order the pack from fastest structural feedback to slowest, so a broken build fails before you spend minutes running tests. cargo check --workspace --all-targets gives the fastest signal: it type-checks every crate and every target (lib, bins, tests, examples, benches) without producing final artifacts, catching the bulk of breakage cheaply. cargo fmt --all --check enforces formatting consistency by failing if any file is not formatted, without modifying the tree, so style never becomes a review argument. cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings is the lint gate; the -D warnings flag promotes lint warnings to errors so the job fails on them rather than letting warnings accumulate unnoticed. cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features then runs the actual behavior checks across every crate, with the same target and feature coverage as the check and lint steps so nothing is exercised under flags the earlier gates never saw.

The flags are not decoration, so justify the ones that matter. --workspace runs the command across every member crate, not just the one you happen to be in, which is the whole point of having a workspace command. --all-targets makes check, clippy, and test look at tests, examples, and benches too, so a test file that no longer compiles or a benchmark with a stale signature is caught in CI rather than the next time someone runs it locally. --all-features compiles the union of feature-gated code so an optional integration cannot rot silently while its feature is off in the default build; note this is a deliberate CI choice and can be heavy, so on large graphs you sometimes split it into a separate job.

Benchmarks are conditional on purpose, because not every repository has a benchmark harness and pretending otherwise produces a CI step that fails on a fresh project. Run cargo bench only when benches actually exist, and run it for compilation and regression signal rather than as a correctness gate, since timing on shared CI runners is noisy. A reasonable pattern is to gate the step on the presence of a benches directory (or a Criterion harness) and treat its results as informational, keeping correctness gating in fmt, clippy, and test. The pack below is specific enough to paste into a pipeline.
exerciseSolutions.code:
# CI command pack: fast structural feedback first, slower checks after.

# 1. Fastest signal: type-check every crate and every target.
cargo check --workspace --all-targets

# 2. Formatting consistency, fail without rewriting files.
cargo fmt --all --check

# 3. Lint gate: warnings become hard failures.
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings

# 4. Behavior: run tests across the whole workspace, every target and feature.
cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features

# 5. Benchmarks ONLY if a harness exists; informational, not a gate.
if [ -d benches ]; then
    cargo bench --workspace
else
    echo "no benches/ directory; skipping benchmarks"
fi
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A paste-ready pipeline ordered from cheapest feedback to slowest, with benches gated on existence.
criteria: The pack includes cargo check, cargo test, cargo fmt --check, and cargo clippy.
cargo bench is guarded by a check for an existing benches directory rather than assumed to be present.
--workspace, --all-targets, and --all-features are each explained: run across all crates, include tests/examples/benches, and compile feature-gated code so it cannot rot.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
none = Err("choose exactly one backend")
s3 = Ok("s3")
local = Ok("local")
both = Err("choose exactly one backend")
labSolution.explanation:
The starter version checks s3 first, then local, and falls through to a vague "not configured" error. That has two bugs that mirror the feature-matrix problem from the chapter: it silently accepts the both-on case (it returns Ok("s3") and ignores local entirely), and its error message does not describe the real constraint. Treating two independent booleans as if exactly one is set is precisely the bad assumption Cargo features make when used as mutually exclusive modes.

The fix matches on the tuple (s3, local) so every combination is handled explicitly. (true, false) selects s3, (false, true) selects local, and the wildcard arm covers the two remaining cases — (false, false) and (true, true) — returning the same explicit error "choose exactly one backend". The match arms are exhaustive over the four boolean combinations, so there is no fall-through ambiguity and no impossible state slips past unvalidated.

Running main calls the function with all four input pairs. (false, false) and (true, true) both hit the wildcard arm and print the error; (true, false) prints Ok("s3") and (false, true) prints Ok("local"). That produces the four lines of expected output exactly, demonstrating the chapter's point at runtime: reject the impossible combinations up front with a clear message rather than assuming the configuration is well-formed.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the operational difference between a package and a crate?
reviewAnswers.answer: A package is what Cargo manages from a single Cargo.toml; it is the unit of versioning, publishing, and dependency declaration. A crate is what the compiler builds in one compilation pass and is the boundary the visibility system works against, where pub means visible to other crates. One package can produce more than one crate (for example a library crate plus several binary crates), but each crate is a single thing the compiler emits, while the package is the manifest-level grouping Cargo operates on.

reviewAnswers.question: When should you create a new crate instead of a new module?
reviewAnswers.answer: Create a new crate only when it buys a real boundary: dependency isolation (so the new crate can avoid or contain dependencies the rest cannot), compile-time separation, reuse behind a stable public surface, or a clean public/private split enforced by the crate boundary. If the only goal is tidier names or folder organization within the same dependency set, a module is cheaper, because it adds no Cargo.toml, no version bump, and no incremental-build cost. Start with fewer crates than your instincts suggest and split when independent dependencies or release policy actually diverge.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is pub(crate) often a better default than pub?
reviewAnswers.answer: pub(crate) lets an item be used freely throughout your own crate while keeping it invisible across the crate boundary, so it never becomes part of your external API. Full pub is a promise: once another crate imports a path, widening was easy but narrowing it again is a breaking change you must support and version. Visibility is a ladder you should climb only as far as a real caller forces, and starting at pub(crate) preserves the freedom to rename or restructure internals, shaping the public surface deliberately with pub use re-exports instead.

reviewAnswers.question: What kinds of choices belong in Cargo features, and what kinds usually belong in runtime configuration?
reviewAnswers.answer: Cargo features suit additive, compile-time choices: optional integrations, platform-specific plumbing, optional dependencies, and extra instrumentation, all expressed so that enabling a feature adds a capability rather than removing one. They are resolved once for the entire build graph before the compiler runs, so they cannot represent anything that varies per environment or per request. Operational mode questions like which database backend a service uses today belong in runtime configuration (an environment variable or config file parsed into an enum), because that decision differs across deployments and the feature resolver cannot express a per-deployment or mutually-exclusive choice safely.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should benchmarking be explicit rather than assumed?
reviewAnswers.answer: Not every repository has a benchmark harness, so a CI step that runs cargo bench unconditionally will fail on a fresh project that has no benches. Benchmark timing on shared CI runners is also noisy, which makes it a poor correctness gate compared with fmt, clippy, and test. The honest approach is to run benchmarks only when a harness actually exists (gating on a benches directory or a Criterion setup) and to treat the results as informational signal for compilation and regression, rather than pretending every repository already has benchmarks in place.

reviewAnswers.question: When should Cargo.lock be committed, and what does workspace.dependencies centralize?
reviewAnswers.answer: Commit Cargo.lock for binaries and services so production builds resolve the exact same dependency graph every time; that reproducibility is the point of the lockfile. Library crates also keep a lockfile in the repository for their own CI sanity, but it does not pin anything for downstream consumers: a library cannot fix its consumers' versions because each consumer resolves the full graph from its own set of dependencies, so the library's lockfile only governs its own CI build. workspace.dependencies centralizes dependency versions and feature sets in the workspace root Cargo.toml, so every member crate opts in with serde = { workspace = true } instead of repeating a version. That keeps the whole workspace agreeing on one version of each shared crate and turns a version bump into a single edit rather than a hunt across manifests.
